decode.claim: The United States has entered the biggest oil deal in history, taking majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, more than doubling American oil reserves, substantially lowering gas prices, and at no cost to the American taxpayer.
decode.source: Trump social-media post, Aug 28; structure briefed by a US official
decode.verdictNote: Framing, and the load-bearing distinction is where reserves are counted. Oil reserves are booked to the ground they sit in, not to the nationality of the shareholder — 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan proven reserves stay Venezuelan reserves under every accounting convention, and what Washington describes buying is 55% of a new company's effective output, split between an equity stake and the right to buy barrels at cost. That is a claim on production, not title. “No cost to the American taxpayer” is also narrower than it sounds: it means no appropriated cash this year, not no sovereign risk on a 100-year concession under an interim government installed after the US removed its predecessor.
decode.reality: Trump announced the deal on social media on Aug 28 and named Marco Rubio, Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodríguez as the negotiators. A US official describes a joint venture with a private Venezuelan company covering 17 fields, a 100-year lease over 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, and a 55% US share of effective output split between ownership and at-cost purchase rights, with at-cost barrels going to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and the military. Venezuela is currently producing about 1.23m barrels a day — its highest since February 2019 — of which Chevron's joint venture accounts for roughly 260,000. For scale on the reserves claim: US proved crude and lease-condensate reserves were 46.4bn barrels at end-2023 (EIA), so 65bn is indeed the larger number, which is exactly why adding it across a border is the move worth catching.
decode.aspiration: No agreement text has been published. The private operator has not been officially named (reporting points to Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt). Nobody has said how the 55% divides between equity and at-cost rights, who funds the roughly $100bn of investment Rubio cited, or which sanctions authorisation lets a US government entity hold the stake. Venezuela's constitution treats hydrocarbons as inalienable public domain and no National Assembly ratification has been shown. Chevron and ExxonMobil both declined to comment — no major has committed capital. On prices: energy analysts Amy Myers Jaffe and Kevin Book both say the infrastructure work takes years and billions, and will not move the pump price this weekend.

angles.effect: Gains an energy-price story and a below-market SPR refill before the midterms, bought with an announcement rather than an appropriation — the cheapest possible instrument, and the reason it arrived as a post rather than a treaty.
Converts a transitional mandate into a governing one: recognition, sanctions relief and a promised $100bn of capital, paid for by pre-committing decades of the country's principal asset.

The concession runs through a private company, so operatorship of what a US official called the world's second-largest private oil company by reserves lands with one businessman rather than a state entity — while Chevron and Exxon pay nothing and say nothing, which is the correct position while the legal text, the sanctions carve-out and the arbitration clause are all missing.

angles.party: Venezuelans and any future elected government
angles.effect: Carry the bill. They inherit a contract they did not vote on, and a dilemma: honour it and a century of the resource is spoken for; break it and sanctions and the security question come straight back.

The party absent from the announcement. If Venezuelan heavy sour genuinely reaches Gulf refiners in volume, the Canadian heavy discount widens — Alberta pays part of the price of a Washington announcement and gets no seat in it.

clock.d90: Sentiment, not molecules. Production stays near 1.2–1.3m b/d and there is no measurable pump-price effect. The testable event is the signing session Caracas says is scheduled for next week, and whether a document appears with it.
clock.m18: The capital question resolves. Either an OFAC authorisation and a published contract exist and a major commits real money, or the deal stays a press release with a lease number attached. Watch whether output moves toward the stated 1.5m b/d.
clock.y7: Where 65bn either becomes barrels or does not. Orinoco extra-heavy crude needs upgraders, diluent, power and port capacity that do not exist at the claimed scale today — and this is also where political durability is tested, when a Venezuelan government that did not sign this has to decide whether to honour it.

watch: The published contract text — its governing law and arbitration seat, the legal name of the joint venture and the identity of the private operator. Its absence is currently the single biggest hole in the claim.
An OFAC general licence or amended sanctions authorisation covering the venture — without one, no US major can lawfully fund it.
A Venezuelan National Assembly ratification vote or gazette publication, given the constitution's inalienable-public-domain clause.
A first at-cost cargo delivered into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, with a dated bill of lading and the price paid versus market.
Venezuelan monthly production in OPEC secondary-source figures crossing 1.5m b/d.
decode.easy: The president said America now controls 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's oil, that it costs you nothing and that it will lower fuel prices. No signed contract has been published, the oil stays in Venezuelan ground under Venezuelan law, and getting it out takes years — so today this mostly helps the government in Caracas that needs the money and the private company that gets to run the fields.

decode.claim: Venezuela preserves ownership of and sovereignty over its resources under a 25-year agreement that returns $19 from every barrel sold to the US, worth up to $209 billion.
decode.source: Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela's acting president, televised address
decode.verdictNote: Partly true, and the half that survives matters: Venezuela does keep legal title, because what Washington describes acquiring is a stake in a company plus purchase rights, not ownership of rock. Both governments can be telling the truth about that at the same time. What they cannot both be right about is the term — Caracas says 25 years, Washington says a 100-year lease — and the money does not reconcile either: 1.5m barrels a day at $19 a barrel is roughly $10bn a year, so $209bn is only reachable as a multi-decade cumulative total, not an annual one.
decode.reality: Rodríguez said in a televised address that the deal covers 17 strategic oilfields with an initial production target of 1.5m barrels a day plus eight greenfield blocks, that $19 from every barrel sold to the US flows to Caracas, and that Venezuela retains “ownership of and sovereignty” over its natural resources “while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise.” She said agreements would be signed the following week. Venezuela's actual output today is about 1.23m b/d, with a government target of 1.37m by year-end — so 1.5m is an increase, not a transformation.
decode.aspiration: The 25-year term is asserted, not documented, and is directly contradicted by the US description of a 100-year lease. The $209bn figure, the $100bn of inbound investment, the eight greenfield blocks and the signing itself are all forward-looking. No text has been published, no National Assembly ratification has been reported, and the constitutional question — whether an inalienable public-domain resource can be committed this way at all — is untouched in her address.

angles.effect: Turns an interim mandate into a sovereignty-preserving national win and gets a fiscal number, $19 a barrel, that she can put in a budget speech. The word 'sovereignty' is doing the political work the term sheet cannot.

angles.party: The PSUV base and the Chavista tradition
angles.effect: Asked to accept foreign operatorship of the industry Chávez nationalised. 'Ownership retained' is the formula that makes that survivable inside the party — which is precisely why it was the first phrase in the address.
Boxed in. Opposing the deal means opposing sanctions relief and $100bn of investment; supporting it means blessing terms negotiated by a government seated after a US operation removed the last one.
Gains by conceding the word. Control of output was always the object, so letting Caracas keep the language of sovereignty costs nothing and stabilises the counterpart it needs to sign.

angles.party: Venezuelan citizens and every government after this one
angles.effect: Pay the spread. They receive $19 a barrel while the venture keeps the rest of the value chain, and they carry the difference between a 25-year commitment and a 100-year one — a gap of three generations that nobody has put in writing, agreed to by an unelected acting president on television.

clock.d90: The signing session Caracas promised. The only thing that matters is whether a stated term appears in a document — 25 or 100 — and whether the National Assembly touches it.
clock.m18: Whether $19-a-barrel receipts actually appear in Venezuelan fiscal accounts, and whether output moves from 1.23m toward the stated 1.5m b/d.
clock.y7: Whether the term survives a change of government in Caracas or of administration in Washington. A concession is paper until an institution enforces it.

watch: The stated term in the signed text — the one number that settles the 25-versus-100-year contradiction between the two announcing governments.
Whether the $19 per barrel is structured as royalty, tax or profit share, and whether it is indexed to price.
A National Assembly ratification vote or publication in the Gaceta Oficial.
A Venezuelan budget line showing receipts from the venture, in the next fiscal presentation.
Whether the eight greenfield blocks appear in the same instrument as the 17 producing fields or in a separate, later one.
decode.easy: Venezuela's acting president said the country keeps ownership of its oil, that the deal lasts 25 years and pays Venezuela $19 a barrel. The ownership part is fair — but Washington described the same deal as a 100-year lease, and the $209 billion she cited only works as a total over decades, not per year.

decode.claim: The violence in the West Bank villages of Qusra and Jalud was criminal, committed by a handful of rioters who are violating the law and harming Israel's standing in the world.
decode.verdictNote: The condemnation is real and unusually direct from this prime minister — but the load-bearing word is “handful,” which recasts a documented and recurring pattern as isolated deviance. The follow-through so far is evidentiary rather than prosecutorial: the military impounded vehicles for a police file, and no arrests were announced. Yesh Din's monitoring of 1,701 police investigations since 2005 finds 93.8% closed with no indictment and only 3% ending in conviction, so a statement and a case file are not the same object.
decode.reality: Dozens of settlers descended on Qusra on Saturday after nearly three weeks of tension, throwing stones at residents and barricading themselves inside a house with Palestinians still in it; in nearby Jalud settlers attacked a Palestinian family and an NBC News crew. The army removed settlers from the Palestinian home, separated the groups, and confiscated vehicles suspected of having been used to reach the area as evidence for a police investigation. Netanyahu's statement was issued the same day and is a rare rebuke.
decode.aspiration: Everything downstream of the words. No arrests were announced, no suspects named, no indictments filed, no administrative orders issued against Israeli citizens for these incidents. Nothing in the statement names an instrument — no policing change, no deadline, no minister tasked. Whether the impounded vehicles produce identified suspects is the open question, and the base rate says most such files close as “offender unknown”.

angles.effect: Buys international cover at zero coalition cost. Words carry no price with his partners; and note the injury he names is to 'the law-abiding Jewish community' and to 'Israel's standing in the world' — the framing is reputational, not about the people who were attacked.
Lose nothing. The statement stops precisely where a coalition fight would begin: it names no policy, no ministry and no enforcement target, so the national-security portfolio is untouched.

Handed an expectation without new authority or a deadline. The statement even describes the army as being 'interfered with' — casting the force responsible for order in the territory as the aggrieved party rather than the accountable one.

angles.party: Residents of Qusra and Jalud, and the reporters covering them
angles.effect: Pay in full and in advance. They face recurring attacks and a 93.8% no-indictment rate, which is the number that actually predicts their next year — not the sentence read out in Jerusalem. An NBC crew was attacked alongside them, and unpunished attacks on journalists mean fewer journalists in those villages, which erodes the evidence base condemnations depend on.

angles.party: European and US officials weighing settler sanctions
angles.effect: Handed the counter-argument. A prime-ministerial condemnation is the strongest available case for holding off on designations — which is a benefit to Israel's government whether or not a single indictment follows.

clock.d90: Whether the Qusra and Jalud files produce named suspects and indictments, or close. This is the only window in which the statement can be falsified cheaply.
clock.m18: Whether the 2026 indictment and conviction rates move off their twenty-year band. One prosecution is an anecdote; a shift in the percentage is a policy change.
clock.y7: Whether any enforcement architecture in Area C changes at all — jurisdiction, police staffing, or the standing of Israeli civilians under military versus civil law.

watch: A named indictment with a case number arising from the Qusra or Jalud incidents.
Whether the impounded vehicles yield identified suspects, or the files close on “offender unknown” — the disposition of those specific vehicles is the cheapest available test.
Any administrative detention or restraining order issued against Israeli citizens for these attacks.
Yesh Din's next data sheet and the 2026 closure and conviction percentages.
Whether the national security ministry publicly backs, contradicts or slow-walks the police investigation.
decode.easy: Israel's prime minister called the settler attacks on two Palestinian villages criminal, which he rarely does. But so far the army has only impounded some cars and nobody has been arrested — and over twenty years, 94 out of every 100 of these police files have closed with no charges at all.

decode.claim: The prompt reaction of Niger's defence and security forces contained the mutiny and gradually regained control of the sites attacked in Niamey.
decode.source: Niger junta statement read on state television
decode.verdictNote: Partly true — and the tell is inside the wording. A government that held its capital does not need to announce that it “gradually regained control” of sensitive sites; the sentence concedes the sites were lost before it claims they were recovered. Containment itself looks real — the state broadcaster came back on air, and the presidential guard repelled an attempt on the palace — but a diplomatic source told AFP the guard retook the air base “with the help of the Russians,” which, if confirmed, means the regime's own forces were not sufficient. That is the part of the day that has consequences, and it is not in the statement.
decode.reality: Sustained gunfire and explosions were reported on Aug 29 around Base 101, the presidential palace and the state broadcaster in Niamey. Soldiers from the Base 101 barracks opened fire on several sensitive sites after attempting to detain fellow soldiers. Télé Sahel went off air for about an hour before being restored around 10:00. Security sources confirmed an attempted breach of the presidential palace was pushed back by the presidential guard. This is the latest challenge to Abdourahamane Tiani, who took power in the 2023 coup.
decode.aspiration: Almost every operational detail. No casualty figures, no confirmed arrests, no confirmation of airport status, no named plotters, and — the absence that matters most — no dated public appearance by Tiani himself. The Russian assistance rests on a single anonymous diplomatic source and has not been confirmed or denied by Niamey or Moscow. “Contained” is a claim about a moving situation made by the party with the strongest interest in it being over.

angles.effect: Survive the day and acquire a licence for a purge of the officer corps — the standard post-mutiny move, and the one that tells you how frightened they actually were. Watch the arrest list, not the statement.

angles.party: The mutineers, reported as junior officers
angles.effect: If they are named and tried publicly, the regime is confident. If the files stay sealed and the men disappear into detention, it is not — secrecy after a failed coup usually indicates the plot reached higher than the government wants known.

angles.party: Russia and its Africa Corps presence
angles.effect: If the air base really was retaken with Russian help, Moscow converts a security service into standing political leverage over Niamey — over uranium contracts, over basing, over what Niger can refuse later. Protection is the most expensive thing a weak government can accept, and France and the US, already expelled from their Niger bases, have no instrument left to compete for it.

angles.party: The Sahel alliance partners, Mali and Burkina Faso
angles.effect: A wobble in Niamey wobbles all three. Their juntas rest on the same arithmetic of junior officers with weapons and grievances, and each attempt raises the perceived odds for the next — as it does for the uranium buyers repricing supply risk who were consulted by nobody.

Pay in curfews, communications cuts and a security establishment that now has to watch itself as well as the jihadist insurgency in Tillabéri — attention diverted from the threat that actually kills them.

clock.d90: Arrests, a military tribunal, and a reshuffle of the general staff or the presidential guard command. Also whether Tiani appears in person, on a dated broadcast — the cheapest proof of control there is.
clock.m18: Whether the purge stabilises the army or seeds the next attempt, and whether any Russian role formalises into a written basing or training agreement.
clock.y7: The base rate governs. Niger has now seen repeated coups and attempts; a regime that survives by purging its officer corps tends to meet the same event again, and each round narrows the pool of officers it can trust.

watch: A published list of arrested officers and the convening of a military tribunal — names and ranks, not a numbered total.
Tiani appearing in person on state television, with a verifiable date.
An official Nigerien or Russian statement confirming or denying Russian participation at Base 101 — the single missing document that would change the read of the whole day.
Reopening of Diori Hamani international airport and a return to published flight schedules.
Changes to the command of the presidential guard or the army general staff in the next gazette.
decode.easy: Soldiers attacked the presidential palace and an air base in Niger's capital, and the government says it contained the mutiny and took the sites back. Saying you “gradually regained control” admits you lost them first — and a diplomatic source says Russian forces helped, which would mean the government now owes Moscow for its own survival.

track.note: No forecasts resolved yet. The first resolve late September (Brent band, Sep 24) into October (Xi summit and the Chinese-bank sanctions question, Oct 1). Every score lands here as it happens — the misses included.

plumbing.read: The buffer is gone and the official gold bid has stopped caring about price. ON RRP sits at $0.17B, the Fed balance sheet is quietly expanding, and central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes of gold in the very quarter gold suffered its worst fall since 2013. But the milkshake tape — oil AND dollar rising together — is still NOT printing: the broad dollar is soft at 118.1, down 2.4% on the month, and that is the live evidence against escalation. Pressure sits in the plumbing, not yet in the price.
plumbing.epoch: E6 still open — the Sept-2019 repo confession never closed — running alongside E7, the weaponized-settlement rail opened by the 2022 reserve freeze that the record official gold bid is a late chapter of.

series.note: the short end the Fed is buying

easy.bottomLine: The board got wider tonight rather than hotter. Iceland is counting a razor-thin vote on whether to restart talks about joining the European Union, a flood on the Nepal-China border has left almost 3,000 people missing and wiped out Nepal's only road to Tibet, and Iran still says the Strait of Hormuz stays shut. Nothing new blew up - but four different parts of the world got harder to fix.
easy.risk: Held at the same level as this evening. The Gulf did not change: Iran repeated that it is in no rush to reopen the strait. What changed is how many places are on the board at once - a European vote that could reshape the EU's northern edge, a disaster that cut a country's trade route in half, and another day of settler attacks in the West Bank that even Israel's prime minister called criminal. None of it crossed a line that forces anyone's hand tonight.
easy.markets: The one number that decides whether oil calms down is not a government announcement - it is what an insurance company charges a tanker for a single trip through the strait. That price has not come down, and Iran just gave insurers a reason to keep it high. Nepal separately lost 431 megawatts of power generation, which turns a country that wanted to sell electricity back into one that has to buy it.
brief: Iceland voted on whether to restart talks about joining the European Union, and the early count is almost exactly 50-50. It matters because Iceland sits in the middle of the North Atlantic between America and Europe, and it is shopping for shelter at a nervous moment.

A wall of ice, rock and water came down a Himalayan gorge and destroyed the only road connecting Nepal to China, along with several power plants. Nearly 3,000 people are missing, and the country just lost a big chunk of the electricity it was planning to sell.

Iran said again that the strait is still shut and it is in no hurry to open it, even though the US said the mines are cleared. Whoever gets to decide when it opens can charge for it, and right now that is Iran.

Israeli settlers attacked two Palestinian villages and a news crew, and the prime minister called it criminal - which he almost never does. But police seized three cars and announced no arrests, so watch what they do, not what he says.

The US president says America now controls 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's oil, and Venezuela's government reportedly handed over rights lasting 100 years. Still nobody has named the oil fields or the company, and no signed agreement has been published.

actors.w: A deal-brander who treats military force as leverage, not doctrine.
actors.g: A visible 'reopened Hormuz, no forever-war' win before the midterms.
actors.m: Called off Iran strikes a fifth time since April, pending a Hormuz deal.
actors.l: Threatens maximally, then delays — the 'decapitation' line is a price tag, not a plan.

actors.w: Career global-macro trader — ex-Soros, broke the Bank of England in 1992.
actors.g: Prove economic warfare can replace kinetic escalation; own the signature policy.
actors.m: Launched 'Economic D-Day' — sanctioning 60 entities across five Iranian lifelines.
actors.l: He is trading Iran's economy like a short position — make every counterparty pre-emptively de-risk.

actors.w: Longtime China/Iran hawk repositioned as the administration's off-ramp diplomat.
actors.g: Land the Hormuz deal that justifies pausing strikes.
actors.m: Told counterparts there will be no new strikes 'for the time being'.
actors.l: The pressure-release valve — when Rubio talks progress, strikes are being deferred.

actors.w: Trump loyalist comfortable as a direct presidential envoy, not a neutral analyst.
actors.g: Deter a Russian move on NATO; recruit Moscow's leverage over Tehran.
actors.m: Made a rare unannounced Moscow trip (Aug 25-27) as the US asked Kyiv to hold long-range strikes.
actors.l: The CIA channel is where the Ukraine and Iran boards secretly connect.

actors.m: Unseen for ~6 months; reportedly wounded in the Feb strike; promised footage never delivered.
actors.l: He may be a legitimacy token the IRGC holds in reserve, not a ruler. (Opacity max; exile-sourced.)

actors.w: Career diplomat and JCPOA architect, trusted by securocrats yet fluent with Washington.
actors.g: A face-saving off-ramp that reopens Hormuz without formal capitulation.
actors.m: Kept the negotiation's public face all summer; reportedly admitted he has lost direct contact with Mojtaba.
actors.l: The shock-absorber — his lost-contact admission is the clearest on-record crack in the leadership fiction.

actors.w: Founding Quds Force commander, Interpol-wanted over the 1994 Buenos Aires bombing; a shadow-war operator.
actors.g: IRGC-institutional primacy — keep the Corps' grip on the state and the Hormuz revenue machine.
actors.m: Anchored the August wartime reshuffle that seated a new security committee.
actors.l: With the Leader invisible, Vahidi's IRGC is the actual center of gravity.

actors.g: De-escalation and economic relief; keep the elected government from IRGC eclipse.
actors.m: Signaled the odds of the war widening have decreased; co-signed the August security reshuffle.
actors.l: He governs the economy and the funerals, not the war.

actors.w: The politician who spent a career warning of Iran and finally got a US president to strike it.
actors.g: Political survival and a victory narrative on Iran and Lebanon without rupturing Washington.
actors.m: Squeezed between a war-favoring electorate and US restraint as re-election nears.
actors.l: Read every Iran decision through the 2026 Israeli election calendar.

actors.w: A hawkish Likud loyalist whose authority is political alignment with Netanyahu.
actors.g: Keep maximum military pressure and preserve the option to re-strike Iran.
actors.m: Warned that 'soon we will be required to act again' during the strike lull.
actors.l: The cabinet's designated hawk-voice — the political floor under any ceasefire.

actors.w: KGB officer turned 25-year ruler who sees the war as civilizational, not transactional.
actors.g: Regime survival fused with a maximalist claim — Ukraine out of NATO, recognized gains, a weakened West.
actors.m: Let Peskov declare talks in 'deep pause' while forces press Pokrovsk without an off-ramp.
actors.l: He negotiates only when compelled; battlefield momentum is his diplomacy. A pause is pressure, not fatigue.

actors.w: Long-serving mouthpiece whose words are calibrated Kremlin temperature-setting, not personal position.
actors.g: Nothing of his own — transmit Putin's framing and manage expectations.
actors.m: Voiced the Aug 28 'deep pause, no new proposals' line, rejecting the joint Western plan.
actors.l: Read him as a thermostat, not an actor. A denial is data; a pause is a posture.

actors.w: The most centralized Chinese ruler since Mao; a recent military purge pushed back his Taiwan timetable.
actors.g: National rejuvenation and a stable US truce that buys time to lock in structural advantages.
actors.m: Publicly defiant on Iran sanctions while preserving the Sept 24 summit and the tariff truce.

actors.w: Xi's chief foreign-policy enforcer; when Wang Yi speaks it is not just the FM talking.
actors.g: Land a smooth, deliverable-laden September summit without blowing the truce.
actors.m: Ran summit-prep diplomacy — met the US ambassador Aug 27, urged both sides to overcome obstacles.
actors.l: He carries Xi's authority, so his positive-agenda push is a real signal Beijing wants the summit to hold.

actors.w: Wartime leader managing a domestic corruption shock and total coalition dependence.
actors.g: Sovereignty and guarantees with no legal recognition of lost land — an armistice, not a treaty.
actors.m: Backed the joint Western plan Moscow just 'deep-paused'; kept striking Russian logistics.
actors.l: He must say yes to Washington and no to surrender at once — his room shrinks as Pokrovsk bleeds.

risk.line: Held at ELEVATED - the board widened tonight without any single theater escalating. The Gulf is unchanged and that is itself the story: Tehran's line carried into Aug 30 unaltered, with deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi saying the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and Iran in no hurry to reopen it, and Iran repeating it will rely equally on diplomacy and defence. Around that, three items moved. Iceland closed polls on restarting EU accession talks, with the first 87,000 of roughly 270,000 eligible ballots running 51.2% yes to 48.8% no and a reliable result not expected before Sunday midday. The Nepal-Tibet flood's missing count climbed toward 3,000 while Nepal's grid operator put 431 MW of lost generation and 470 MW of damaged projects under construction on the books, with the Rasuwagadhi crossing - the only overland link to China - destroyed. And settlers attacked Qusra and Jalud in the northern West Bank, drawing a rare condemnation from Prime Minister Netanyahu, three vehicles seized and no announced arrests. Ukraine's two open clocks from this evening - Zaporizhzhia on emergency diesel and the Bucha-district depot detonation that killed at least 37 - are unresolved and sit on the watch list rather than the cards. No chokepoint changed hands, no nuclear or NATO line was crossed.

forecasts.q: US commits to fixed Venezuelan heavy-crude export infrastructure (Orinoco/Maracaibo dredging or a dedicated terminal)
forecasts.note: The Aug 28-29 deal hands a new operator control of ~65bn barrels — about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves — and reporting frames it plainly as an alternative to Gulf crude routed through Hormuz. Straight on geography: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz, the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean tanker routing to Gulf-Coast refineries plumbed for heavy sour crude. But fixed infrastructure would be the premeditation tell — you do not dredge channels for a prize seized by accident. Unconfirmed as of Aug 29; opportunistic harvest remains the live alternative

forecasts.q: Hormuz transits recover past 50% of pre-war volume
forecasts.note: Transits rose 30% week-on-week to 114, and the same week JMIC counted single-digit vessels a day — both true, both about a tenth of the 130/day baseline. Mine clearance and insurance re-rating are physical clocks: Suez took roughly a year to clear after 1974

forecasts.q: Brent stays inside the $80-100 band
forecasts.note: Brent 88.29, a fourth quiet mid-band session and -5% on the week. Band survival is realized vol times remaining time, and with 26 days left both terms improved; both tails weakened too

forecasts.q: Israel-Hezbollah escalates to multi-week campaign
forecasts.note: Two months on, Israel says the Lebanese army has fallen short on dismantling Hezbollah infrastructure. Fortna: ceasefires with an agreed verifier hold far better, and this one still has none while the party being disarmed rejects the premise

forecasts.q: China stands up a third physical-gold venue or a delivery-forcing mechanism
forecasts.note: Central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes in Q2, up 62% year on year, in gold's worst quarter since 2013. Infrastructure follows official flow — but record buying is not venue construction, and this is the weakest of today's moves

forecasts.q: Hormuz at full pre-war normal
forecasts.note: The same clock argument at a harder threshold, plus Washington discarding the June MoU terms removes the ready-made text a full normalization would have been built on

forecasts.q: China quarantine or blockade of Taiwan
forecasts.note: A record 244 Chinese state ships around Taiwan in July doing seabed survey work Taipei reads as anti-submarine mapping, while fighter sorties sit at a three-year low. Precondition-building, capped by the PLA purge pushing the timetable right

hypotheses.name: IRGC captured the succession (weak form — assessed finding)
hypotheses.d: Documented pressure on Assembly electors, 8 boycotts, overridden shortlist and will. The pre-arranged-pact version scores only 30% — the plan was overridden, not executed.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — 75% → 82%
hypotheses.d: Week's biggest mover, on three strands independent of the Israeli/exile channel. Pezeshkian said on Iranian state TV that communication with Khamenei is 'very difficult' — Tehran's own president, against his own interest. Washington routed its peace offer not to Araghchi but to Mohsen Rezaee, career IRGC commander-in-chief now running the security council. Cipher Brief: 'Tehran isn't saying who is actually in charge.' Capped at 82% because the state has promised footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders — that is the falsifier, and it is coming.

hypotheses.name: Nobody’s hurrying on Hormuz — HELD at 60%
hypotheses.d: The near-breakthrough-then-condition pattern fired a sixth time (Iran–Oman interim corridor and 30–60 days of technical talks, against Ghalibaf restating the full condition stack). Deliberately not moved: it is already priced, and a minesweeping calendar is what an honest process looks like too. The real test is live — the offer sits with the IRGC, so Tehran's answer is the experiment.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — 55% → 60%
hypotheses.d: The discriminating split signal arrived: PLA sorties kept declining while the coast guard escalated in kind — CCG 2307 pressing a Japanese coast guard ship in the strait Aug 6–10, which AEI reads as testing whether foreign vessels will obey PRC authority. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up is the ratchet signature. Capped at +5; the stated tell is what the coast guard does through the Sept 24 visit.

hypotheses.name: NEW · Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it opens at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts, and the reporting frames it in plain words as an alternative to Gulf oil routed through Hormuz. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Operation Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Mundane alternative, named and live: drugs, migration politics, regime-change, with the barrel a bonus. Falsifiers — cut hard if export volumes stay token (the $2-2.8bn tranches are a rounding error against control of 65bn bbl), if Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing does not actually swing off the Middle East, or if the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appears. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz, geography does not work that way — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Real Orinoco or Maracaibo channel-dredging and dedicated heavy-crude terminals WOULD be the premeditation tell. Unconfirmed today; it is the thing to watch.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — 45% → 52%
hypotheses.d: Economic Outcast hit ~60 teapots, tankers and traders and touched no Chinese state major and no bank — Treasury sent the majors a warning letter instead. Maximum pressure on Iran, calibrated to stop exactly short of anything that would detonate the Sept 24 summit. Held to +7 because the Munir offer is a real concession, and $4.10 gas before midterms is real evidence against premeditation.

hypotheses.name: NEW · A pre-announcement leak into oil futures
hypotheses.d: Four times in the war window, nine- and ten-figure short bets landed 15–20 minutes before an Iran announcement: ~$2.2bn across crude, gasoil and gasoline before Trump's Mar 23 pause post; ~$950m before the Apr 7 ceasefire; ~$760m before Iran said Hormuz would open. ~$7bn total; CFTC probing, four members of Congress demanding answers. Split: deliberate leak 45 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 25 / coincidence 10. This is the only entry in the book whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event rather than pattern-matched after — which is why it opens this high. Against it: no episode has surfaced around this week's diplomacy.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 30% → 25%
hypotheses.d: Cut again. The channels that actually moved this week were Oman, Pakistan and the new Mecca defence pact — Russia was absent from every one of them, and still has not offered the mediation this hypothesis expects. Motive 9/10, documentary evidence 0/10, pre-event evidence never. Cut to 15% if nothing surfaces by Sept 30.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Both its live predictions came in favourably this week and it gets credit for neither: the rival leverage hypothesis predicted the same things, and shared predictions are ambience. One more failed pre-summit call and it goes to the epitaph list.

brief.h: Iceland is counting a knife-edge vote on reopening the EU door, and the argument is really about the krona
brief.t: Polls closed Saturday on an advisory referendum asking whether Iceland should restart European Union accession negotiations frozen since 2013. Early partial counting of the first 87,000 ballots, out of roughly 270,000 eligible voters, ran 51.2% yes to 48.8% no; officials said a reliable result might not arrive before midday Sunday, and more than 63,000 people had voted before polling day. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir called it a great day and said her government would continue its work whatever the outcome; opposition leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir said these are not problems Brussels will solve, they are problems Icelandic politicians must solve. The foreign ministry estimates talks could open by end-2026 and run 18 to 24 months, with a second referendum on actual membership years later.
brief.context: The connective move: this is a monetary-sovereignty vote wearing a fisheries coat. Iceland's policy rate is 8.00% against the ECB's 2.25%, and that spread is the yes campaign's real argument - a tiny economy running its own floating currency pays a permanent risk premium on every mortgage and every import, and the euro is the only instrument that removes it. The no campaign's asset is physical rather than monetary: accession eventually routes quota-setting through the Common Fisheries Policy, and fish are the export base, so the fight is over who writes the catch limits. The rail predates the headline - Iceland applied in 2009 in the wreckage of its banking collapse and shelved the bid in 2013 once the krona stabilised, which means the application has always tracked currency credibility rather than ideology. Name the deciding desk: not Brussels but the Althingi, because the vote is advisory and any real bid needs a parliamentary majority that survives the fishing lobby. The second theater is security - Iceland has no standing army, sits astride the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap, and is shopping for shelter at a moment when Washington's Arctic posture has made small North Atlantic states nervous, which is why a country already inside the EEA and Schengen would still want the seat it currently lacks. Base rate, and it cuts against excitement: EU accession referendums mostly pass, but advisory ones won inside a two-point margin rarely convert into fast treaty movement. Falsifier: a formal Icelandic application letter lodged in Brussels before Dec 31.

brief.h: The flood that erased Nepal's only overland road to China also took 431 megawatts off its grid
brief.t: A landslide of ice and rock about 20km northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing triggered a debris-laden flood down the Lhende river and into the Bhote Koshi gorge on the morning of Aug 26, according to an initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery. The flood destroyed the Rasuwagadhi border post, bridges, hydropower plants and stretches of the only road linking Kathmandu to Tibet overland. At least 676 people have been killed in Nepal and seven in Tibet, with the missing count rising toward 3,000 by Aug 29; more than 100 people were reported trapped inside the Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Rasuwa. The Nepal Electricity Authority says the damage removed an estimated 431 megawatts from the grid and damaged projects under construction totalling 470 megawatts. The missing include pilgrims and trekkers bound for Mount Kailash and foreign nationals - reporting cites roughly 90 Americans, 41 Australians and nine South Koreans working at a hydropower site.
brief.context: Constraint before character: Nepal is a landlocked state with exactly two ways out - India, and one road to Tibet - and this flood took the second one. That is why a natural disaster is a geopolitical event and not only a humanitarian one; the Rasuwagadhi-Gyirong crossing is the physical expression of Kathmandu's decade-long attempt to hold an alternative to Indian leverage, and it is now rubble. Follow the money and you see why the casualties cluster in construction camps: Nepal's growth strategy is hydropower built for export to India, which means the country monetises the same steep glacier-fed gorges that generate this hazard - the asset and the risk are physically the same object. So 431 MW off a grid this size is not an outage, it is a strategy setback: it converts a would-be exporter back into an importer, and the seller is Indian. The deciding desks are the Nepal Electricity Authority for the grid and, for the corridor, the Chinese side of the crossing, because only Beijing can reopen its half and it therefore sets the timetable. Prefer the boring explanation over any design read - this is exposure siting, not sabotage. Base rate: the same Lhende stream flooded in July 2025 and ice-rock and glacial-lake outburst events across this range have been recurring, so this is a repeat on a known hazard rather than a freak, and rebuilt Himalayan infrastructure historically goes back on the same alignment. What would change the read: whether the crossing reopens in months rather than a year, and whether reconstruction moves the road and the powerhouses off the gorge floor.

brief.h: Tehran says out loud what the insurance market already said: the mine-free declaration bought nothing
brief.t: Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and that Tehran is in no hurry to reopen it. The IRGC separately stated it maintains firm control of the strait and accused US officials of making false statements about the passage in order to move energy prices - an allegation, not an established fact. This lands three days after CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper declared the internationally recognized transit routes free of Iranian sea mines and the President issued his own all-clear on Aug 26. Nothing in the overnight cycle moved it: Iran's stated posture into Aug 30 was that it will rely equally on diplomacy and defence to protect its interests.
brief.context: The connective move is that the declaration and the reopening were never the same decision, and this week both parties to the disagreement said so. Reopening is priced by war-risk underwriting committees in London and by the protection-and-indemnity clubs whose cover a tanker needs to call at most ports; they held their rates when Washington announced the all-clear, and Tehran has now supplied the exact sentence that justifies holding them. Follow the incentive rather than the rhetoric: a strait that is legally shut but physically passable is worth more to Iran than either a closed one, which invites strikes and kills its own exports, or an open one, which returns nothing. Keeping the reopening date in Tehran's gift is the Sound Dues logic - Denmark grew rich for four centuries not by closing the Danish straits but by making passage a permission rather than a right. The deciding desk is Iran's Supreme National Security Council with the IRGC Navy as operator, not the foreign ministry that reads it out. Base rate: insurance markets lag political all-clears by months, and verified clearance after both the 1974 Suez effort and the 1987-88 Gulf campaign ran on multi-month clocks. Falsifier, dated and public: published war-risk rates falling back under 3% of hull value before Oct 31 would mean underwriters bought the declaration anyway and the permit-regime read is wrong.

brief.h: Netanyahu condemned the Qusra attack in unusually sharp words, and then the state seized three cars
brief.t: Dozens of Israeli settlers descended on the Palestinian village of Qusra in the northern occupied West Bank on Saturday after nearly three weeks of tension in the area, throwing stones at residents and barricading themselves inside a house with Palestinians inside, according to residents and the Israeli military. In nearby Jalud, settlers attacked a Palestinian family and a foreign news crew accompanying them; an NBC News team was reported among those attacked. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a rare condemnation, saying he strongly condemned "the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel's standing in the world." Security forces seized three vehicles; no arrests were announced.
brief.context: Read the statement as a desk output rather than a moral event, and parse the harms he actually named: injustice to the settler community, interference with the IDF, damage to Israel's standing abroad. The Palestinians attacked are the setting of that sentence, not its injured party - which tells you the audience is foreign governments and the army, not the villages. The constraint is coalition arithmetic: the ministries controlling the police and the West Bank civil administration sit with the settlement bloc, so a prime minister can condemn while the enforcement chain runs through people with no incentive to indict. That is why the operative number is arrests rather than adjectives, and three vehicles seized with no arrests announced is the base rate rather than the exception - Israeli rights monitors have documented for years that settler-violence files overwhelmingly close without indictment. Name the mechanism: privatised coercion, where displacement is produced by actors the state can disown, so no official ever signs the order that empties a hillside. The honest alternative reading is that this is genuine irritation at a specific breakdown - settlers physically obstructing the IDF is a real institutional grievance, and that alone can explain the language with no strategy behind it. What would change the read, dated: indictments filed against named Qusra or Jalud participants within 30 days, or administrative detention orders used against settlers on the terms they are routinely used against Palestinians.

brief.h: The Venezuela deal now comes with a reported 100-year term, and still no named field, company or published instrument
brief.t: The President announced on Aug 28 that the United States had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves across 17 Venezuelan fields at no cost to the American taxpayer, working through Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth with Venezuelan interim president Delcy Rodriguez and a private partner. Subsequent reporting says the Rodriguez government granted rights over those reserves running 100 years; Rodriguez called the agreement historic and framed it around recovery of hydrocarbons infrastructure, while Rubio framed it as securing stable reserves and low-cost oil. Figures attached to the arrangement include about $100bn of investment and over $209bn in future taxes to Caracas. Trump said the deal more than doubles US reserves, currently around 46 billion barrels. Oil researcher Rory Johnston called the 65-billion-barrel figure a red herring with little relevance to actual deals, saying the relevant details remain almost entirely unknown. Neither government has published an official text, and no fields or operating companies have been named. Reporting identifies Alejandro Betancourt Lopez, co-founder of Derwick Associates, as the key intermediary.
brief.context: The gap between Venezuela's roughly 303 billion barrels of proven reserves - about 17% of the world total - and its roughly 1% share of world output is the entire story, and it is a physical fact rather than a political one. Orinoco crude is extra-heavy: it needs diluent, upgraders and coking capacity before it becomes a sellable barrel, which is why reserves in the ground have never converted into flow without roughly a decade and tens of billions in capex. So the announcement is not about barrels arriving; it is about who holds title when they eventually do - and a hundred-year term is the tell, because you write a century into a contract precisely when you expect the counterparty government to change. Follow the money and the mechanism is the return of the concession: a private vehicle rather than a state-to-state treaty routes around PDVSA's litigated balance sheet and around any need for Congressional appropriation, which is what no cost to the American taxpayer actually encodes. The desks that decide are OFAC, which must write the license architecture before a cargo moves legally, and the reserve-based lending banks, who will not finance production against a title no court will defend. Base rate, and it is unkind: every foreign oil concession in Venezuela has been renegotiated or nationalised - 1976 and again in 2007 - and announcements that precede signed instruments convert at a far lower rate than announcements that follow them. Falsifier: a published OFAC general license naming fields and operators, plus a Venezuelan legal instrument, before Dec 31.

lecture.title: The Economic Weapon: Why Sieges Make the Wars They Mean to Prevent

sections.t: Treasury designated roughly sixty Chinese “teapot” refiners — the small plants buying discounted Iranian crude — while touching no Chinese state major and no bank. The same week, central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes of gold in the quarter gold fell over 20%. Two stories, one machine.

sections.h: Follow the money, name the mechanism
sections.t: A reserve manager buying into a 20% drawdown is not trading. He is hedging ACCESS — the risk that an asset held abroad gets switched off by its host government — and gold is the only large reserve asset with no counterparty who can flip that switch. Name the mechanism: the ECONOMIC WEAPON, using the financial plumbing whose hubs one country owns to inflict a siege without laying one. Iran discounts crude to Chinese teapots paying through dollar-touching chains; Treasury designates them; the IRGC's Strait Authority recoups the shortfall in Hormuz tolls. Sanction and gold bar are one transaction seen from two ends.

sections.h: Deep history I — the blockade that became an idea
sections.t: The economic weapon has a birthday and a founding failure. The birthday is November 1806, when Napoleon's Berlin Decrees declared the British Isles blockaded — the Continental System, an attempt to beat a maritime power by closing a continent's markets to it. It succeeded at nothing except generating enforcement. Portugal would not comply, so France invaded in 1807 and got the Peninsular War, the ulcer that bled the Grande Armée for six years. Alexander I quit the system in December 1810 because it was ruining Russian trade, and in 1812 Napoleon marched east to enforce it. The blockade never defeated Britain; it manufactured the two wars that destroyed the blockader. Sanctions require enforcement, and enforcement against a determined leakage path tends toward conquest. The second case mattered because it worked. The Allied blockade of Germany ran from 1914 through the armistice and was lifted only when Germany signed at Versailles in June 1919. German official estimates put civilian deaths from malnutrition near 424,000 — contested, and historians still argue how much was blockade and how much German agricultural mismanagement. But perception makes policy, and a generation concluded hunger had beaten an undefeated army. So they institutionalized it as a PEACE instrument: Article 16 of the League Covenant made sanctions automatic against an aggressor, and Wilson in 1919 put it in words no Treasury official would dare use today — “A nation that is boycotted is a nation that is in sight of surrender. Apply this economic, peaceful, silent, deadly remedy and there will be no need for force.” The weapon was invented to ABOLISH war; the rest of the century refutes that sentence.

sections.h: Deep history II — the failures that define our problem
sections.t: ABYSSINIA, 1935. Italy invaded Ethiopia; the League invoked Article 16 — exempting oil, coal and steel, and never closing the Suez Canal, which Britain controlled and through which Italian troopships sailed. Mussolini won anyway. The sanctions were real enough to enrage and too porous to stop, and the lesson is sharper than “sanctions don't work”: a sanction calibrated to spare the sender teaches the target that the sender is deterred too. Then the second-order effect. Nicholas Mulder's argument in The Economic Weapon is that the interwar regime deterred small states and PROVOKED large ones. Italy, Germany and Japan drew the same conclusion from the 1930s — dependence on seaborne trade was a vulnerability an enemy could switch off at will, and the answer was autarky, self-sufficiency taken by force. Lebensraum and the Co-Prosperity Sphere were ideological projects; they were also sanctions-proofing programs. Japan is the proof case. Washington embargoed scrap iron in 1940, then froze Japanese assets on 26 July 1941; America supplied roughly 80% of Japan's oil, and with Britain and the Dutch East Indies following, Japan lost about 88% of its oil imports. Reserves would last three years at peace, half that at war — Nagano's image was of a patient wasting away, every month of compliance leaving Japan weaker against the enemy it expected to fight. Pearl Harbor came in December. And the detail that turns story into discipline: the freeze was never meant to be total. Roosevelt intended a licensing regime keeping oil flowing so the tap stayed usable as leverage; officials in State and Treasury administered it so strictly that no licences issued and the flow stopped. The sanction that helped produce Pearl Harbor was substantially an organizational outcome, not a presidential decision — Allison's Essence of Decision, live. Before inferring “Iran's strategy” from one action, ask which bureau took it.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: The leakage path is always the whole story — not the designation list, the leak: Portugal and Russia in 1806, Beira and Pretoria in 1966, Chinese teapots now. NOW THE BREAK. Japan in 1941 had a military option that promised to SOLVE its resource problem: seize the Dutch East Indies and own the oil. Iran has none — it fought its war, lost the conventional exchange, and has played its asymmetric card, the Hormuz toll. Nor did 1914 face an alternative supplier: Iran's is the world's second-largest economy, which the sanctioner just spared. Less Pearl Harbor, more Rhodesia.

MULDER says the siege provokes: strangulation drives large states to autarky, then preemption. DREZNER says sanctions are cheap theater — Hufbauer's data give a third success rate at best, near zero against great powers. The 2026 evidence buries neither: it splits by SIDE, and the split is the finding. On the TARGET Mulder scores: gold, stockpiles, payment rails, enrichment acceleration under maximum pressure. On the SENDER Drezner scores harder — the carve-outs. Sixty teapots and not one bank is not escalation; it is the sanctioner taking its own threat hostage, because hitting a Chinese bank endangers the dollar system that makes the hammer heavy.

The 2015 architecture is not coming back (high confidence): the 2022 freeze of Russian reserves turned the settlement network into an instrument; a hedge once bought is not resold. Expect bifurcation, not de-dollarization (moderate-high). EICHENGREEN is right that currencies erode glacially; the WEAPON depreciates faster than the CURRENCY. The bolder call (moderate): the most dangerous decade is the one in which the weapon still works but no longer terrifies. Mulder's mechanism fires in the transition — invested in escaping, not finished, expecting strangulation regardless. For China, the 2030s — so Economic D-Day may SHORTEN the fuse it was meant to lengthen. FALSIFIER: designate a major Chinese state bank; if Beijing cuts Iranian purchases within a quarter, I am wrong. Two centuries say the economic weapon does not replace war — it sorts the world into blocs that survive each other's sieges, then gives the survivors a reason to fight.

Nicholas Mulder, The Economic Weapon (2022) — published weeks before the Russia sanctions matched its template. Farrell & Newman, “Weaponized Interdependence” (2019) — it called the 2022 playbook and the chip controls in advance. Eichengreen, Exorbitant Privilege — the counterweight.

fired: None today. Every named wire was checked against its threshold and none met it - logged deliberately so the non-fire is scoreable.

No new attack at the strait since the Kuwaiti tanker Al Salam II was holed above the waterline on Aug 26, already logged on the 27th. Nothing met the stricter wording either: a US-flagged or US-escorted vessel, or an attack Iran publicly claims.

Near-wire, not fired: the record 244 Chinese government ships around Taiwan is the same gray-zone ratchet the Taiwan wire watches, but that wire's threshold is mobilization-type activity and survey hulls are not it. Not counting it is the discipline; saying so is the record.
armed: Any attack on a US-flagged or US-escorted vessel - the sharpest open escalation trigger
Israeli strike inside Iran during the corridor talks
A Kremlin confirmation of a September negotiating round - a reversal out of the deep pause
Ferry requisition, reserve mobilization or missile dispersal near Taiwan
Scholar-owned: IRGC/Basij defection (Takeyh) - casualty-recruitment crossover (Kofman) - PLA purge tempo (Fravel)

watch: Iceland's full count by Sunday midday, then whether a two-point advisory yes actually produces an application letter lodged in Brussels before Dec 31 - the Althingi decides that, not the referendum
Whether published war-risk premia fall back under 3% of hull value - the London underwriting committee, not CENTCOM, sets the real reopening date, and Tehran has now told them not to bother
Whether the Rasuwagadhi crossing reopens in months rather than a year, and whether Nepal's 431 MW of lost generation gets rebuilt on the same gorge floor that just took it out
Whether an OFAC general license naming Venezuelan fields and operators, or any signed Venezuelan instrument, follows the 65-billion-barrel and 100-year claims - paper, not adjectives, is the tell

Whether arrests and indictments follow the Qusra and Jalud attacks within 30 days, and whether Zaporizhzhia's diesel resupply keeps pace with its burn rate while Ukraine's depot audit stays unpublished
